title: Tailored isolation and metabolomic profiling of extracellular vesicles in Manila clam (Ruditapes philippinarum) hemolymph and insights into water-derived vesicles
content:
by Valentina Moccia, Giulia Dalla Rovere, Thi Tran Ngoc Minh, Andrea Zendrini, Marije Kleinjan, Marc C. Roelofs, Paola Berto, Claire M. Labrie, Tzviya Zeev-Ben-Mordehai, Esther A. Zaal, Paolo Bergese, Annalisa Radeghieri, Massimo Milan, Marca H. M. Wauben, Valentina Zappulli

Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are evolutionarily conserved mediators of intercellular communication released by cells into biological fluids and the environment. Despite their increasing relevance in biomedical and veterinary research, knowledge of EVs in marine bivalves remains limited. This study first aimed to optimize protocols for EV isolation from the hemolymph of Manila clams (Ruditapes philippinarum) using density gradient ultracentrifugation (dgUC) or size exclusion chromatography (SEC). EV-enriched fractions were identified and characterized for nanoparticle size distribution by nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), for protein concentration and imaged by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and cryo-EM. Small EVs (<200 nm) were successfully purified with both methods. While dgUC provided higher-purity preparations, SEC provided higher particle-yields and compatibility with metabolomic analyses. Metabolomics performed on SEC fractions and hemolymph revealed a distinct metabolic signature of EV-enriched fractions, characterized by metabolites associated with nucleotide metabolism, glycolysis, redox regulation, and energy metabolism. Secondly, in a separate pilot study, we investigated the presence of EVs in water conditioned by Manila clams. EVs were concentrated by tangential flow filtration and ultrafiltration and characterized by NTA, atomic force microscopy, TEM and by CONAN assay to assess their purity. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of EV-recovery from conditioned water but also the need for methodological refinement and appropriate controls to improve EV purity and distinguish EVs released from clams or from other organisms. Overall, these preliminary results establish a foundation for future investigations into the role of EVs in bivalve biology and their application as minimally invasive biomarkers for aquaculture and environmental monitoring.
